bp: A programming class needs feedback that is timely, specific, and fair. A student submits Python code, runs into failing tests or confusing error traces, and needs to know what to fix next without waiting days for a human grader. Large language models are attractive here because they can read code and produce natural-language comments, but the task is not just chatting about code. The system must compare a student's submission with rubric criteria, test cases, and error evidence, then turn that comparison into feedback that is correct enough to guide learning. This paper asks how such feedback systems should be organized. Should one carefully written prompt ask the model to judge the whole rubric at once, or should several model-based agents each judge a narrower part? The practical goal is dependable automated assessment for student programming work, where vague or biased comments can mislead learners rather than help them.
wh: The hard part is that feedback generation asks one system to hold several different objects in mind at the same time: the student's code, the expected behavior from test cases, the meaning of error traces, and the separate requirements listed in a rubric. These objects do not always point in the same direction. A program may pass some tests but still show a misunderstanding. An error trace may reveal one bug while the rubric asks about a broader concept. Feedback also has to be pedagogically useful, not merely judgmental. Existing single-prompt systems can overwhelm the model because the prompt asks for many judgments in one pass. That can produce generic comments, inconsistent scoring, or bias reinforced by whichever part of the prompt dominates the model's answer. But splitting the work across agents is also risky: separate judges may disagree, duplicate effort, or lose the full context needed to make useful comments.
naive: A smart beginner would put everything into one instruction: here is the student's code, here are the tests, here is the error trace, here is the rubric, now write feedback for every criterion. This is simple and easy to deploy. It also keeps all evidence in one place, so the model can in principle connect a failed test to a rubric item. The failure is overload. When many criteria compete inside one response, the model may skim, collapse distinct rubric items into one generic note, or favor visible symptoms over the deeper programming issue. A second naive idea is to create one agent per criterion and combine their answers. That reduces local overload, but it can fragment the assessment if the agents do not share enough context or if their separate judgments are hard to reconcile.
ap: The paper's central move is to treat automated feedback as an evaluation architecture question rather than assuming that more model calls automatically mean better teaching. It compares a traditional single-prompt setup with a multi-agent design in which different agents assess distinct parts of the rubric or assessment criteria. The input is multimodal in the practical sense used by the abstract: several kinds of evidence are brought together, including student-written code, test cases, error traces, and rubric criteria. The study then examines whether splitting the task produces more precise, correct, and consistent feedback than a well-designed all-in-one prompt. It also evaluates the evaluators themselves by studying language models used as judges, including multiple-judge strategies. The important finding is cautious: the abstract reports that well-designed single-prompt setups often generate more actionable and personalized feedback than multi-agent approaches.
mech: The mechanism begins with a concrete programming-assignment record. The system receives the student's erroneous Python code, the tests associated with the task, any error traces produced by running the code, and the rubric criteria that define what the feedback should cover. In the single-prompt condition, these materials are packed into one carefully designed instruction, and one model produces feedback across the rubric. In the multi-agent condition, the assessment burden is divided: individual agents are assigned distinct aspects of the criteria, so each agent focuses on a smaller question. Their outputs then have to be treated as parts of a larger feedback judgment, either by comparison, aggregation, or downstream evaluation. The paper runs this comparison across several open-source language models, with model sizes from 20B to 70B parameters, on an open-source dataset of 57 Python programming tasks containing student error code and associated test cases. It measures feedback precision, correctness, and consistency across architectures. A second layer judges the generated feedback itself: the study tests language models as evaluators and multi-judge strategies, asking whether model-based judging can reliably tell which feedback is more specific and useful.
math: The main mathematical object is a scoring problem over uncertain judgments. The system must decide whether a piece of feedback matches the evidence in the code, the tests, the error trace, and the rubric. Precision means the comment points to the relevant issue instead of making broad claims. Correctness means the comment is faithful to what the program and tests show. Consistency means similar evidence should lead to similar judgments across runs, criteria, or evaluators. A single-prompt design asks one model to make a joint decision: it must weigh all criteria together and choose a response that balances them. A multi-agent design decomposes the joint decision into smaller subdecisions, one per aspect, then combines the resulting signals. That is the idea of dividing a hard judgment into parts, but it creates a tradeoff between focused scoring and lost shared context. The evaluation layer uses agreement as evidence: if several judges independently rate feedback similarly, their shared signal may be more trustworthy than one judge. But agreement is not truth by itself. Judges can share the same bias, especially when they are language models trained on similar data or prompted in similar ways.
dots: This paper connects to the conference's broader language-model and agent work because it studies where control should be placed around a fluent but unreliable text generator. Many agent papers ask whether splitting work into roles, tools, memories, or judges improves reliability. This paper shows that the answer can be no when the split weakens the full view of the task. It also connects to learning-from-examples work: the system is not hand-coding every possible bug, but reusing patterns from model training and assignment evidence to produce feedback for new submissions. It touches evaluation and ranking as well, because generated feedback must be compared by quality, not merely produced. The family-level lesson is that language-model systems need checks, but a check is useful only when it measures the right thing. More agents, more judges, or larger models do not remove the need to define what counts as actionable, correct, and consistent feedback.
ww: The single-prompt setup can work well because feedback is often a context-heavy judgment. A student's code, the failed tests, and the rubric criteria may only make sense when read together. If one carefully written prompt keeps that whole situation visible, the model can connect a specific error trace to the relevant rubric item and phrase feedback in a way that fits the student's actual code. The multi-agent setup has a plausible advantage: each agent faces a narrower question, so it should be less distracted by unrelated rubric parts. But the abstract's result suggests that this advantage is not guaranteed. When agents see only slices of the assessment, they may miss cross-criterion relationships, repeat generic advice, or produce comments that do not combine into a coherent teaching message. The work therefore explains reliability as a balance between focus and shared context. A good single prompt may beat a poorly coordinated agent team because it reduces confusion while preserving the whole evidence bundle.
po: The payoff is practical guidance for building automated programming-feedback systems. The study does not simply ask whether language models can produce feedback; it compares architectural choices under evidence from code, tests, error traces, and rubrics. It uses open-source models from 20B to 70B parameters and an open-source set of 57 Python programming tasks, making the comparison more concrete than a prompt anecdote. Its reported result is especially useful for educators and tool builders: a well-designed single-prompt approach may produce more actionable and personalized feedback than a multi-agent design. That can save cost and engineering complexity while improving consistency, if the prompt is carefully built and evaluated.
limits: The abstract is cut off, so the exact metrics, full result details, and all experimental conditions are not visible in the input. The study uses 57 Python tasks, which gives concrete evidence but does not prove the same outcome for every programming language, course level, rubric style, or student population. The result also depends on prompt design and agent coordination; a different multi-agent design might behave differently. Model-as-judge evaluation must be treated cautiously because judges can share blind spots with the systems they evaluate. The work assumes that test cases, error traces, and rubric criteria are available and meaningful. If those inputs are incomplete or misleading, neither a single prompt nor an agent team can reliably produce trustworthy feedback.
